q: how does a jet engine work
detailed explanation of how a jet engine works
how does a jet engine work step by step
a: A jet engine works on the principle of Newton's third law (for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction) using a four-step process called the Brayton cycle: intake, compression, combustion, and exhaust. Step 1 — Intake: Air enters the engine through the front fan (the large fan visible at the front of the engine). This fan pulls in large volumes of air. About 80% of this air bypasses the core of the engine and flows around it, creating most of the thrust in modern turbofan engines (the type used on commercial airliners). The remaining 20% enters the engine core. Step 2 — Compression: The incoming air passes through a series of compressor stages made up of rotating blades (rotors) and stationary vanes (stators). Each stage compresses the air further, increasing its pressure by up to 40 times (40:1 pressure ratio). This compression heats the air to around 500°C. Step 3 — Combustion: The compressed air enters the combustion chamber where fuel (kerosene) is injected and ignited. The burning fuel-air mixture reaches temperatures of up to 2000°C. This hot, expanding gas wants to rush out of the engine. Step 4 — Exhaust: The hot gases pass through a turbine section, which extracts energy to drive the front compressor and fan. The remaining high-velocity gas exits through the nozzle at the back, creating thrust. The key difference between a turbojet and a turbofan is the bypass ratio — modern high-bypass turbofans move a large volume of air around the core, making them more efficient and quieter than pure turbojets. Jet engines are most efficient at high altitudes and high speeds, which is why planes cruise at 35,000+ feet.
